one_line_contribution: A stress test claiming that time-based forgetting (recency decay, usage-utility pruning, bounded-FIFO consolidation) in LLM-agent experience stores deletes exactly the records a dormant ALFWorld task family needs when it returns, so that the return-block loss exceeds the stationary savings, exceeds the loss from random pruning at the same store size, is not closed by re-learning, and is avoided by a time-agnostic redundancy/coverage prune at the same size — with a token accounting showing decay and consolidation maintenance is net-negative.
closest_prior_work: Verified by s2cli: arXiv:2604.27003, 'When Continual Learning Moves to Memory: A Study of Experience Reuse in LLM Agents' (2026-04-29, 3 cits) — its stated finding is that memory-augmented LLM agents face continual-learning problems at the retrieval level and that memory design choices trade off transfer against forgetting. That is the proposal's thesis in general form; the proposal's advance is narrowed to 'which deletion criterion, measured at a scheduled return.' Second threat, also verified: arXiv:2606.02461 AgentCL (2026-06-01), which supplies controlled task streams plus transfer/stability metrics for language agents and ships MemProbe (filters unreliable experience during consolidation). Continual-learning evaluation frameworks conventionally re-evaluate earlier tasks — that is a return measurement under another name — so a reviewer will ask what the 'return block' adds beyond backward transfer already in AgentCL's protocol, especially since the proposal itself calls AgentCL 'a possible protocol to adopt.' Third: arXiv:2605.09315 (verified), 'Do Self-Evolving Agents Forget?', which documents capability erosion under memory evolution and proposes a preservation constraint; the proposal's differentiator (attributing erosion to a specific deletion criterion) is real but incremental over it. Beyond the literature, the closest threat is internal: the program's own appendix already contains breadth_routed_memory, 'Consolidate the Broad, Retrieve the Narrow: Coverage — Not Utility, Not Usage — Decides Where Agent Experience Should Live' (5.35), whose conclusion is verbatim this proposal's constructive claim; the brief explicitly forbids restating the 27 ideas, and this proposal does not say how it goes past that one.
strongest_objection: The headline result is entailed by the policy definitions, not discovered by the experiment. Every policy is forced to the same 30% cap, and the policies differ only in which records they drop: F1 and F2 score records by recency and by retrieve-count-times-success (the proposal states 'dormant records fall to zero'), so at a 70% deletion rate they must delete family-A records after five intervening blocks; F4 clusters embeddings and keeps a medoid per cluster regardless of age, so it must retain family-A representatives. P1 ('F1/F2 below F5 at return, F4 within MDE') therefore cannot come out any other way, and P3 (reinserting the deleted A records recovers the deficit) is a consistency check on the retrieval pipeline rather than a test of the hypothesis. What is left as genuinely uncertain is only P2, P4 and P6 — and P6, the no-return control, is the single real falsifier in the set. A skeptical AC will read this as 'LRU is bad under cyclic access,' a result from caching theory, re-measured on ALFWorld. Compounding it, the effect-size arithmetic does not close: this program measures the whole retrieval channel at about +0.6 points on the 27B, the pre-registered MDE is about 5 points net at n≈415 pooled, and P1 is a family-A-restricted claim on roughly 69 probes per family (≈207 pooled over three rotations), where MDE is larger still. A store worth a couple of points cannot produce a family-restricted deficit that clears a ~5-point MDE, so the most likely outcome is that every prediction lands inside the noise band and the paper reports nothing. The pre-gate checks that F5 minus no-memory clears MDE on the probe overall; it does not check that the family-A slice can support the confirmatory test.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Kill the by-construction objection by making the comparison one of degree rather than of definition: add a decay policy with a coverage floor (decay normally but never let any cluster/family fall below one retained record) and show that the floor, not the abandonment of time, is what recovers return performance — that turns 'replace time with redundancy' into a testable claim with an interesting negative branch. (2) Fix the statistics before the design: report a pilot-measured family-A store value (F5 minus no-memory restricted to family A on the 120B) and set the confirmatory arm's n from it, or drop family-restricted claims and pre-register the pooled post-return delta as the primary endpoint; a design whose primary prediction is smaller than its own MDE is not runnable as written. (3) Give the return block a no-memory floor arm so a deficit can be located between 'lost the useful record' and 'regressed to memoryless.' (4) Run at least one policy at its native, uncapped size — FadeMem is not run at a 30% cap, and forcing it there makes the whole comparison an artifact of the harness rather than a statement about the published methods. (5) Cut scope: one rotation, one backbone, the cap sweep dropped, WebShop dropped, in exchange for enough seeds for the return block to clear noise.
missing_baseline: A decay/usage policy with a coverage or per-family retention floor — i.e. the obvious cheap patch to F1/F2 that keeps the temporal criterion and only forbids a family from reaching zero. Without it, the claim 'replace time-since-use with redundancy' is never tested against 'keep time-since-use and add a floor,' which is what any practitioner reading this would actually implement, and which a reviewer will point out is a one-line change to FadeMem. Secondary omission: a no-memory (store-off) arm scored on the A-prime block itself; the pre-gate uses no-memory only on the probe, so the paper cannot say whether F1's return-block deficit is a memory harm or simple regression toward the memoryless floor. Third: the hindsight oracle F7 is constructed from F5's own A-prime run and so bounds only F5-shaped policies; it gives F4 no fair ceiling.
